The way light lingers in the corners of a room at dusk has always fascinated me—the way it softens edges and makes everything feel temporary, like a brushstroke fading into canvas. There’s something poetic in impermanence. A coffee cup left overnight, its dusty rim; a bookmark slipped between pages, but the book was closed months ago. These small, forgotten things carry stories, though they belong to no one now.

I wonder if the world is made of these echoes—moments that hum when we’re not listening. Like how stepping into an empty hallway makes the acoustics feel different, or how a half-remembered song plays just beneath thought’s surface. Maybe we’re all haunted by fragments of things we’ve lost or never possessed.

Time, too, is a shape-shifter. Sometimes it drags like molasses, other times it sprints ahead, leaving us stumbling in its dust. The paradox of aging is that you stop noticing the years until, suddenly, they’re shouting at you. Yet in between, there are these quiet pockets where the world pauses, where a raindrop could last forever if you let it.

I think about how trees grow so slowly they outlive empires, while a single mayfly burns bright for a day. What does any of it matter in the grand, indifferent scheme? Only that we try to care, to imprint a little meaning where none was before. Even that’s fleeting.

But perhaps fleeting is the only kind that matters.
